1.pericope_label: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God

schools.summary: Gill hears in the opening clause an allusion to the Israelites being encompassed with the pillar of cloud, or with the clouds of glory the Jews speak of in the wilderness. The looking he insists is not with bodily eyes, since Christ is not now to be looked upon in that manner, but with the eye of the understanding or of faith — a spiritual sight of Christ which is at first but glimmering and afterwards increases, of a soul-humbling nature, marvellous and surprising, transforming into his image and filling with joy unspeakable; a believer should be always looking to Christ and off every other object, as the word used here signifies. Christ is to be looked to as a Saviour who, being appointed and sent by God, has become the author of eternal salvation, able and willing to save, a suitable, complete and only Saviour. Calvin treats the conclusion as an epilogue to the previous chapter, showing the end for which the catalogue of the saints was given, that every one should be prepared to imitate them; he calls the large multitude a cloud by a metaphor which he insists is classical and not scriptural, Homer using a cloud of footmen and a cloud of birds and Livy a cloud of footmen and horsemen, what is dense being set in opposition to what is thinly scattered. Had they been few in number, he says, they ought still to have roused us by their example, but being a vast throng they ought the more powerfully to stimulate us, so that wherever we turn our eyes many examples of faith immediately meet us; and he declines to take the word for witnesses in its general sense of martyrs. On the joy he holds the Greek quite clear whatever the ambiguity of the Latin: though it was free to Christ to exempt himself from all trouble and to lead a happy life abounding in all good things, he yet underwent a death that was bitter and in every way ignominious, the phrase meaning instead of joy, and joy including every kind of enjoyment; if any one thinks the preposition denotes the final cause he does not much object, the meaning then being that Christ refused not the death of the cross because he saw its blessed issue, but he still prefers the former exposition.

Henry sets out the duty urged on the Hebrews as consisting of two parts, the one preparatory and the other perfective. The weight to be laid aside he takes as all inordinate affection and concern for the body and for the present life and world: an inordinate care for the present life, or fondness for it, is a dead weight upon the soul, which pulls it down when it should ascend upwards and pulls it back when it should press forward, and makes duty and difficulties harder and heavier than they would otherwise be. The besetting sin he defines by the advantage it holds, being the sin that has the greatest advantage against us by the circumstances we are in and by our constitution.

Clarke summarises the chapter’s argument before commenting, and renders the participle for looking as looking off and on, or from and to — looking off from the world and all secular concerns to Jesus and to all the spiritual and heavenly things connected with him — still an allusion to the Grecian games, where those who ran were to keep their eyes fixed on the mark of the prize and the goal in view. The exhortation implies, he says, both that they should place all their hope and confidence in Christ as their sole helper in this race of faith and that they should consider him their leader and imitate his example. The first title he allows generally signifies captain or leader or the first inventor of a thing, but judges the reference here to be rather to the judge in the games, whose business it was to admit the contenders and to give the prize to the conqueror. Wesley calls the cloud a great multitude tending upward with a holy swiftness, witnesses of the power of faith, and glosses the laying aside from the racecourse, that we throw off whatever weighs us down or damps the vigour of the soul; the besetting sin he specifies threefold, as the sin of our constitution, the sin of our education, and the sin of our profession. The looking he explains by a type, the wounded Israelites looking to the brazen serpent — our crucified Lord prefigured by the lifting up of it, our guilt by the stings of the fiery serpents, and our faith by their looking up to the miraculous remedy — and the two titles he takes of one who begins faith in us, carries it on, and perfects it; the enduring he calls patient and willing, and the sitting down a place where there is fulness of joy.

Barnes analyses the chapter as applying the principles of the preceding one to the readers’ own case, representing the ancient worthies who persevered as witnesses of their strife in the Christian race and cheering them on to victory, and then appealing to the example of the Saviour as a more illustrious instance than any adverted to before, adduced for a separate and special specification rather than listed with theirs. On the two titles he observes that the word our is not in the original and obscures the sense: the meaning is that Christ is the first and the last as an example of faith or of confidence in God, occupying in this as in all things the pre-eminence and being the most complete model that can be placed before us; he had not been enumerated among those distinguished for faith, but is now referred to as above them all. Ellicott renders the verse afresh and remarks that in one so difficult we need an exactness of translation which might not otherwise be desirable; the chief thought, he says, is that we run our race with patient endurance looking unto Jesus, the writer never wearying of enforcing the need of faith and patience in all who would inherit the promises, and the connection is chiefly with the last verses of the previous chapter. He notes that the description precedes the name, that the runner looks away from all other objects and fixes his gaze on One, that Jesus is not directly spoken of as the Judge but has himself reached the goal so that his presence marks where the race will close, and that origination is the principal thought in the first title, which here stands in contrast with the second. Robertson calls the opening particle a triple compound of emphasis found only twice in the New Testament and holds there should be no chapter division here, since these verses are the climax of the whole argument about the better promises and a passionate appeal for loyalty to Christ. The word for cloud he distinguishes from the word for a single cloud, taking it of a vast mass and referring the metaphor to the great amphitheatre; the participle he renders looking away to Jesus, a glance at the cloud of witnesses and then the eyes fixed, since he is the goal. The second title he judges to be a word apparently coined by the writer, found nowhere else, and the clause about the joy he takes in the sense of exchange, the joy lying at the end of the race and the cross at this end, endured while despising a shame that then attached to the most shameful of deaths.

Cyril of Jerusalem, on the sitting at the right hand of the throne of God, gathers the testimonies to it: the word in the Gospel that henceforth they shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power; the Apostle Peter writing of Jesus Christ, who is on the right hand of God, having gone into heaven; the letter to the Romans, that it is Christ that died, yea rather that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God; the charge to the Ephesians about the working of his mighty power which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his own right hand; and the teaching to the Colossians that those risen with Christ should seek the things above.

debates: What the cloud is: Gill takes it for an allusion to the pillar of cloud and the clouds of glory in the wilderness, while Calvin denies the figure is scriptural at all and traces it to Homer and Livy as a classical way of describing a dense multitude, Robertson agreeing that the word means a vast mass of cloud and referring the whole image to the amphitheatre.

Whether Christ is here the exemplar of faith or its source: Barnes strikes the word our from the clause and makes him first and last as an example of faith, set above the worthies of the previous chapter; Wesley reads the same two titles of one who begins faith in us, carries it on and perfects it; Clarke moves him off the racecourse altogether and identifies him with the judge who admits the contenders and awards the prize.

What the clause about the joy means: Calvin prefers instead of joy, so that Christ exchanged an available happiness for a bitter and ignominious death, while allowing without much objection the reading that takes the preposition of the final cause, that he refused not the cross because he saw its blessed issue; Robertson takes the exchange sense outright, the joy at the far end of the race against the cross at this one.
outliers: Robertson protests at the chapter division itself, holding that these verses are the climax of the whole preceding argument and should not have been cut off from it.
Calvin supports a biblical metaphor from pagan poetry and history, citing a cloud of footmen and of birds in Homer and of horsemen in Livy, and expressly denies that the usage is scriptural.
Wesley reads the looking through the brazen serpent and maps three things at once — the lifting up to the crucifixion, the stings to our guilt, and the Israelites’ gaze to our faith.
Ellicott concedes that this verse needs a precision of rendering he would not otherwise think desirable, treating exactness here as a concession to difficulty rather than a general rule.

3.pericope_label: For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin

schools.summary: Gill takes the considering widely: of the greatness of Christ’s person as God, the Son of God and heir of all things; of his offices as prophet, priest and King, as the Saviour of lost sinners and the Leader and Commander of the people; and of his human nature and conversation on earth, pure and holy in his nature, harmless and innocent in his conversation, meek and lowly in his deportment. On the next verse he lists what the readers had already resisted — sin, Satan, the world and the men of it, its lusts and its frowns and flatteries, and the false teachers, every adversary of Christ and of their own souls — but not yet unto blood or the shedding of it, as some of the Old Testament saints had done, and some in the times of the Maccabees, and James the apostle, and Christ himself. Calvin enforces the exhortation by the comparison of Christ with us: if the Son of God, whom it behoves all to adore, willingly underwent such severe conflicts, who of us should dare to refuse to submit with him to the same? This one thought alone, he says, ought to be sufficient to conquer all temptations — that we are companions or associates of the Son of God, and that he who was so far above us willingly came down to our condition in order to animate us by his own example. At the next verse he presses further, that even when the ungodly persecute us for Christ’s sake we are then contending against sin; and he marks the limit of the comparison, since into this contest Christ could not enter, being pure and free from all sin, whereas in this respect we are unlike him, for sin always dwells in us and afflictions serve to subdue it and put it to flight.

Henry takes the exhortation to patience and perseverance as pressed by an argument drawn from the gentle measure and gracious nature of the sufferings the believing Hebrews endured. He owns first that they had suffered much and had been striving to an agony against sin, and defends the conflict on both sides: the cause of it was sin, and to be engaged against sin is to fight in a good cause, since sin is the worst enemy both to God and man; and the warfare is both honourable and necessary, for we are only defending ourselves against that which would destroy us if it got the victory over us, so that we fight for ourselves and for our lives and ought therefore to be patient and resolute. Every Christian, he adds, is enlisted under Christ’s banner to strive against sin — against sinful doctrines, sinful practices and sinful habits.

Clarke asks for more than a comparison: they are attentively to observe and analyse every part of Christ’s conduct, to enter into his spirit and examine his motives and object, and to remember that as he acted they are called to act, since he will furnish them with the same Spirit and support them with the same strength; Christ bore a continual opposition of sinners against himself but conquered by meekness, patience and perseverance, leaving an example to be followed. On the next verse he observes that many of those already mentioned were martyrs for the truth who persevered unto death and lost their lives bearing testimony, whereas these readers, though they have had opposition and persecution, have not been called to seal the truth with their blood; the striving he takes as an allusion to boxing at the Grecian games. Wesley glosses the first verb as drawing the comparison and thinking, and puts it as a question — the Lord bore all this, and shall his servants bear nothing? — takes the contradiction as enmity and opposition of every kind, and reads the warning as being lest they grow dull and languid and so actually faint in their course.

Barnes takes the exhortation as attentively reflecting on Christ’s example in order to bear trials properly, and refers the contradiction to the Jews of the Saviour’s time, who opposed his plans, perverted his sayings and ridiculed his claims, while he, regardless of their opposition, persevered in the course he had marked out and went patiently forward. The general sense of the next verse he gives as a comparison of degree: they have not yet been called in their Christian struggles to the highest kind of sufferings and sacrifices, and great as their trials may seem their faith has not been put to the severest test, so that they ought not to yield in the conflict with evil but manfully resist it; he notes a continuance of the athletic allusion. Ellicott keeps the figure of the race in view, taking the sense to be that unless they look to Jesus they will grow weary, and renders the first verb literally as compare — place your sufferings by the side of his. The word for contradiction he prefers to render gainsaying, and insists it need not be limited to contradiction in words, since the Greek version so frequently uses it of the rebelliousness of the people of Israel. At the next verse he marks a substitution within the same general figure, the contest of the pugilists taking the place of the footrace, so that where sin was first the hindrance to be put aside it is now the antagonist to be subdued; he notes exactly the same transition in the first letter to the Corinthians, and observes that the contest has been maintained but feebly, no blood having flowed in their struggle, though they have not deserted the arena. Robertson calls the first verb an old word meaning to reckon up, to compare and to weigh, found only here in the New Testament, and holds that understanding Jesus is the key to the whole problem and the cure for doubt and hesitation; the participle for enduring he identifies as the same verb used just before, and the word for gainsaying as one already twice used in the epistle. The verb of the next verse he parses as a double compound meaning to stand in opposition against in a line of battle, intransitively to stand face to face against, found only here in the New Testament, and renders the phrase as up to blood, which was true of Jesus and of many of the heroes of faith in the preceding chapter.

Chrysostom observes that there are two kinds of consolation, apparently opposed to one another but yet contributing great strength each to the other, both of which the writer has here put forward. The one is when we say that persons have suffered much, for the soul is refreshed when it has many witnesses of its own sufferings — which is why he had earlier bidden them call to mind the former days in which, after they were illuminated, they endured a great fight of afflictions. The other is when we say that a man has suffered little, which is what is done here.

debates: Whether the contradiction was verbal: Ellicott insists the word need not be limited to contradiction in words, since the Greek Old Testament so often uses it of Israel’s rebelliousness, while Barnes fills it out as the perverting of sayings and ridiculing of claims and Robertson keeps to the lexical history of the term.

What contest the figure changes into: Ellicott and Clarke both make it boxing, Ellicott noting the identical transition of figure in the Corinthian letter, while Robertson takes the verb off the sand entirely and reads it of standing face to face in a line of battle.

How far the comparison with Christ will run: everyone else presses the likeness between his sufferings and theirs, but Calvin marks the point where it fails — that in striving against sin we are precisely unlike Christ, who could not enter that contest at all, being free from the sin which always dwells in us.
outliers: Chrysostom notices two consolations working at once which appear to contradict each other, that a man has suffered much and that he has suffered little, and holds each lends the other strength.
Ellicott observes that the readers have not deserted the arena but have merely shrunk from the blows, no blood having flowed in their struggle.
Robertson makes the whole difficulty of the epistle turn on one thing, saying that understanding Jesus is the key to the problem and the cure for doubt and hesitation.

5.pericope_label: And ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons

schools.summary: Gill allows the opening clause to be read as a question — have ye forgotten? do ye not remember? — and says it would be right to call the consolatory word to mind. On the ground of the chastening he narrows the premise: all men are not the objects of God’s love, only a special people whom he has chosen in Christ, for whom he gave his Son while they were yet sinners and enemies, whom he quickens and calls by his grace, justifies, pardons and accepts in Christ, and causes to love him; these he loves with an everlasting and unchangeable love, in a free and sovereign way. The enduring he takes of the manner as well as the fact, in faith, with patience, with courage and constancy, with humility and reverence, and lists what may encourage it: that it is but a chastening, and the chastening of a father; that it comes from the Lord and is for his glory and their good; and the example of Christ. Calvin reads the first words as a question, since the writer asks whether they had forgotten and thereby intimates that it was not yet time to forget; the testimony he divides into two parts, that we are not to reject the Lord’s correction, and the reason, because the Lord loves. He then raises the objection against the reason himself: this seems not to be a well-founded argument, for God visits the elect as well as the reprobate indiscriminately, and his scourges manifest his wrath oftener than his love, as the Scripture speaks and experience confirms; his answer is that when the godly are addressed, the effect of the chastisements which they feel is alone referred to, however severe and angry a judge God may show himself towards others. At the following verse he reasons from the common practice of men, that it is by no means right or meet that God’s children should be exempt from the discipline of the cross, since no prudent man of sound judgment is to be found among us who does not correct his children — for without discipline they cannot be led to right conduct — and much less will God neglect so necessary a remedy, being the best and wisest of fathers.

Clarke prints the opening clause as a question, and takes the quotation to show that the address in Proverbs, which at first sight appears to be from Solomon to his son, or from some fatherly man to a person in affliction, is properly from God himself to any person in persecution, affliction or distress. The chastening he calls a proof of the fatherly love of God Almighty, showing his most gracious designs towards us, from which we may be fully convinced that the affliction will prove the means of good to our souls if we make a proper use of it — here being the reason why we should neither neglect correction nor faint under it. The enduring he takes of the manner: if they submit to his authority, humble themselves under his hand and pray for his blessing, they will find he deals with them as beloved children, correcting them to make them partakers of his holiness, and acknowledging by it that they belong to the family. Of the last verse he says it proceeds on the general fact that illegitimate children are neglected in their manners and education, their fathers feeling little affection for or obligation towards them, whereas all legitimate children are partakers of discipline; and he observes that the original word does not imply stripes and punishments but the whole discipline of a child. Wesley keeps the indicative in the first clause but softens it, that they seem already to have forgotten an exhortation wherein God speaks to them with the utmost tenderness; the despising he glosses as slighting or making little of the affliction, or imputing it to chance or second causes instead of seeing and revering the hand of God in it, and the fainting as failing to endure it patiently and fruitfully. The reason he reduces to a sentence — all springs from love, therefore neither despise nor faint — and the last verse he qualifies only by adding that all sons are partakers of this more or less.

Barnes identifies the quotation and states its object, that afflictions were designed on the part of God to produce some happy effects in the lives of his people and ought therefore to be borne patiently, the previous verses having pointed to the example of the Saviour. The maxim he takes as a universal rule that God sends trials on those whom he truly loves, guarding it twice — it does not mean that he sends chastisement which is not deserved, nor that he sends it for the mere purpose of inflicting pain, which cannot be, but that by his chastisements he shows he has a paternal care for us. On the condition that follows he is emphatic that it does not mean if you endure it patiently or bear up under it, but if you are chastised or corrected by God, the affirmation relating not to the manner of bearing but to the fact that we are disciplined. The last verse he puts negatively: if they never meet with anything adapted to correct their faults, to subdue their temper or to chide their wanderings, it would prove them in the condition of illegitimate children, cast off and disregarded by their father. Ellicott takes the shrinking from trouble as a shrinking from the chastening every son receives, prefers to render the verb of the quotation as holding converse or reasoning with them as with sons, and notes that the citation agrees with the Greek version except that son appears as my son and reproveth as chasteneth. At the next verse he adds a second textual note: as the words stand in the Hebrew text the meaning is even as a father the son in whom he delighteth, but a very slight change in one word yields the sense in which the Greek translators understood the clause and which is here retained, the difference between the two renderings not being material for the purpose of the quotation. On the condition he reports that the whole weight of ancient evidence favours a change in the first Greek word, after which two translations are possible — that it is for chastening that they endure, the troubles coming upon them being for discipline and not sent in anger but in fatherly love, or simply endure for chastening, bearing the trial instead of seeking to avoid it by unworthy and dangerous concession. The final inference he states as an impossibility: were it possible that they had never known this fatherly chastening, it must be that they are not sons whom a father acknowledges and for whose training he has care. Robertson parses the first verb as a perfect middle of an old word found only here in the New Testament, and the verb of the quotation as an old one meaning to ponder different things and so to converse; the scourging he traces to the word for a whip and remarks that this is a hard lesson for God’s children to learn and to understand. On the condition he takes the same reading as Ellicott and renders it just endure for chastening; the word for the illegitimate he notes is an old one occurring only here in the New Testament.

debates: Whether the opening clause is a statement or a question: Calvin reads it as a question outright, holding that the asking itself intimates it is not yet time to forget, and Gill and Clarke both allow the same, while Wesley keeps the indicative and softens it to seeming.

Whether the maxim states a universal rule: Barnes takes it as one and guards it against two misreadings, while Calvin objects that God visits elect and reprobate alike and that his scourges manifest wrath oftener than love, restricting the statement to the godly as those addressed, and Gill narrows the love itself to a people chosen in Christ.

What kind of condition the next verse states: Barnes insists it concerns the fact of being chastised and not the manner of bearing it; Clarke and Gill both read exactly the manner he excludes, of submission, humility and patient endurance; Ellicott and Robertson prefer a reading with better ancient support which removes the condition altogether.
outliers: Calvin states the objection to his own text plainly, that the reason given seems not to be well founded, since chastisement falls on elect and reprobate alike and more often shows wrath than love.
Clarke observes that the word rendered chastening does not imply stripes and punishments at all but the whole discipline of a child, at home and abroad.
Ellicott makes two textual notes in successive verses and judges the divergence between the Hebrew and the Greek immaterial to the argument the writer is drawing from the passage.
Robertson breaks off the grammar to admit that this is a hard lesson for God’s children to learn and to understand.

9.pericope_label: Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live? For they verily for a few days chastened us after their own pleasure; but he for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness. Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby

schools.summary: Gill explains the title of earthly parents as given because they are the immediate causes and instruments of the generation of their children and of their fleshly bodies and worldly beings, and to distinguish them from the Father of spirits; this, he says, shows that we have not the spirit or soul from them, only the flesh or body, which is frail and corrupt and therefore goes by that name. The few days he takes to respect neither the minority of children, during which they are under a parent’s correction, nor the short life of parents, but rather the end which parents have in chastening, which is their children’s temporal good and lasts but a few days — a sense the opposition in the latter part of the verse requires. The last verse he takes as anticipating an objection drawn from the grief and sorrow that come by afflictions, and answers by granting that no affliction seems to be joyous in outward appearance to flesh and blood and according to the judgment of carnal sense and reason. Calvin sets out the comparison in its several parts: that if we showed so much reverence to the fathers from whom we descended according to the flesh as to submit to their discipline, much more honour is due to God who is our spiritual Father; and that the discipline fathers use towards their children is useful only for the present life, whereas God looks farther, having in view to prepare us for an eternal life. The second amplification he states as the appointment of God’s chastisements to subdue and mortify our flesh so that we may be renewed for a celestial life, from which it appears that the fruit or benefit is perpetual — such a benefit not being expected from men, since their discipline refers to civil life and properly belongs to the present world. The last verse he takes as added lest we should measure God’s chastisements by our present feelings, since we are like children who dread the rod and shun it as much as they can, because owing to their age they cannot yet judge how useful it may be; chastisements cannot be rightly estimated if judged according to what the flesh feels under them.

Clarke observes that the fathers of our flesh, that is our natural parents, were correctors, and we reverenced them notwithstanding that their corrections often arose from whim or caprice; how much rather should we be in subjection to the Father of spirits, from whom we have received both body and soul, who is our Creator, Preserver and Supporter, and to whom both we and our parents owe our life and our blessings. The few days he takes of duration and extends the point: the chastisement of our earthly parents lasted only a short time, and that of our heavenly Father will also be but a short time if we submit, for as our parents ceased to correct when we learned obedience, so will our heavenly Father when the end for which he sent the chastisement is accomplished — God delights not in the rod, and judgment is his strange work. On the last verse he widens the field to correction, wholesome restraint, domestic regulations and gymnastic discipline alike, none of which are pleasant to those exercised by them, but by which obedient children, scholars and great men are made; and it is by God’s discipline that Christians are made, since he who does not bear the yoke of Christ is good for nothing to others and never gains rest to his own soul. Wesley glosses the reverence as neither despising nor fainting under their correction, and the submission as made with reverence and meekness that we may live with him for ever; he suggests that the two expressions may intimate that our earthly fathers are only the parents of our bodies, our souls not being originally derived from them but created immediately. The few days he takes of life itself — how few are even all our days on earth — and the contrast of the two disciplines he states by conceding a fault, that our parents frequently erred by too much either of indulgence or severity, while God always, unquestionably, acts for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness, that is, of himself and his glorious image. The last verse he takes generally, of all chastening whether from our earthly or our heavenly Father, grievous for the present yet yielding the peaceable fruit of righteousness — holiness and happiness — to those who receive the exercise as from God and improve it according to his will.

Barnes derives the argument of the verse from the difference in the spirit and design with which we are corrected by God and by an earthly parent: in God everything is without any intermingling of passion or improper feeling, while in an earthly parent there is often much that is the result of hasty emotion and an irascible temper. The few days he refers to the correction having to do mainly with this short life, so that the corrections of earthly parents had a much less important object than those of God. On the last verse he refuses to soften the pain: all chastisement is intended to produce it, and the Christian is as sensitive to pain as others, his religion not blunting his sensibilities and making him a stoic but rather increasing his susceptibility to suffering — the Lord Jesus probably feeling pain, reproach and contempt more keenly than any. Ellicott marks the transition from likeness to contrast, the previous verses having said that God chastens as a father, and identifies the two terms as our natural parents and the Father of spirits, the Creator of all spirits who is the Giver of life to all; he renders the following clause as seemed good unto them and continues the contrast between human liability to mistake and the perfect knowledge of our heavenly Father, who seeks our profit and cannot err in the means he employs, noting a general resemblance between the two verses in which the few days answers to the fathers of our flesh. On the last verse he prefers a slightly changed reading giving that all chastening seems for the present time to be not joyous but grievous, and holds the language so far perfectly general, relating to all chastening whether human or divine, since with a lower sense of righteousness the maxim is true of the wise discipline of earthly parents. Robertson marks the connective as the next step in the argument, parses the verb as an imperfect of customary action meaning we used to have, and notes that the noun rendered chasteners is an old word occurring once in the Greek Old Testament and twice in the New. The following clause he renders according to the thing seeming good to them, marking the demonstratives set in contrast, and the phrase for the present he identifies as a classical one; the words not joyous but grievous he takes as predicate ablative or predicate genitive, either making sense.

Chrysostom compares the case to bitter medicine: they who drink it first submit to some unpleasantness and afterwards feel the benefit, and such is virtue and such is vice — in vice there is first the pleasure and then the despondency, in virtue first the despondency and then the pleasure. But there is no equality between the two, he insists, for it is not the same thing to be first grieved and afterwards pleased as to be first pleased and afterwards grieved.

debates: What the phrase fathers of our flesh implies about the soul: Gill infers from it that we have the body from our parents but not the spirit, and Wesley suggests the same more tentatively, that our souls are not originally derived from them; Ellicott and Calvin take the words simply as one term of a contrast and press nothing from them.

What the few days measure: Gill makes it the end parents aim at, their children’s temporal good; Barnes the reference of the correction to this short life; Clarke the duration of the correction itself, which he then extends to God’s, ending when its purpose is accomplished; Wesley the brevity of life.

How wide the maxim about chastening runs: Ellicott adopts a slightly changed reading making it general to all chastening, human or divine, and Wesley agrees, while Gill treats the sentence as an answer to an objection about afflictions in particular and Calvin as a caution against measuring God’s chastisements by present feeling.
outliers: Barnes denies that religion makes a man a stoic, holding instead that it increases his susceptibility to suffering, and adds that the Lord Jesus probably felt pain, reproach and contempt more keenly than anyone.
Chrysostom sets virtue and vice in the same order of pain and pleasure reversed, then refuses to let the symmetry stand, since being grieved first and pleased after is not the equal of the opposite.
Clarke draws a limit on God from the analogy, that as parents stop correcting when obedience is learned so will he, adding that God delights not in the rod and that judgment is his strange work.

12.pericope_label: Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees; and make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed

schools.summary: Gill takes the words as spoken to the Hebrews with respect to themselves, noting the Syriac version reads your hands and your knees, and describes them as sluggish and inactive in prayer, in hearing the word, in attendance on ordinances, in holding fast their profession and in performing what adorns it, weary and fatigued with the weights and burdens of sins and afflictions, and faint, fearful and timorous. By feet he understands the walk and conversation of the saints, both in the church and in the world, for which paths are made ready — the good old paths of truth, of the word and worship of God, of faith and holiness — and to make those paths straight is to make the word of God the rule of walking, carefully avoiding to join anything with it as a rule. Calvin explains the connection: having taught that God regards our salvation when he chastises us, the writer now exhorts us to exert ourselves vigorously, since nothing will more weaken us and more fully discourage us than through the influence of a false notion to have no taste of God’s grace in adversities, and nothing is more efficacious to raise us up than the intimation that God is present with us even when he afflicts us and is solicitous about our welfare. To this he adds a second requirement, that we walk prudently and keep to a straight course, for indiscreet ardour is no less an evil than inactivity and softness, and this straightness of the way is preserved when a man’s mind is superior to every distraction.

Henry grants the fact before prescribing the remedy: a burden of affliction is apt to make the Christian’s hands hang down and his knees grow feeble, to dispirit him and discourage him, and against this he must strive that he may better run his spiritual race and course. Faith and patience, he says, enable believers to follow peace and holiness as a man follows his calling, constantly, diligently and with pleasure; and peace with men of all sects and parties will be favourable to our pursuit of holiness.

Clarke refers the exhortation to the prophet and describes those addressed as persons almost worn out with sickness and fatigue, whose hands hang down, whose knees shake, and who are totally discouraged, exhorted to exert themselves and take courage with the assurance that they shall infallibly conquer if they persevere. The straight paths he reads as a choice of road: take the straight path that is before you and do not go in crooked or rough ways where there are stones, briers and thorns by which you will inevitably be lamed and so totally prevented from proceeding, whereas in the even and proper path what was wounded by getting into a wrong way will be healed by moderate and equal exercise, all impediments being removed. Wesley allows the hands to be either your own or your brethren’s, and divides the two members between the two figures — hands unable to continue the combat, knees unable to continue the race. The straight paths he takes as made both for your own and for their feet, every hindrance and every offence being removed, and the lame as those who are weak and scarce able to walk, who must not be turned out of the way of faith and holiness.

Barnes takes the exhortation as following from what has been stated, that afflictions are sent from God and are evidences of his paternal watchfulness, and reads the posture literally: the hands fall by the side when we are exhausted with toil or worn down by disease, so that the summons is to renew courage and make a new effort to bear them, the words being taken from Isaiah. The word for straight he notes means properly straight in the sense of upright or erect, but is used here of straightness in the horizontal sense — level, plain, smooth — the meaning being that they were to remove all obstacles out of the way so that they need not stumble and fall, with a probable allusion to a passage in Proverbs. Ellicott marks the transition from personal risk and duty to what is binding on all members of a community, and renders the first verb as strengthen, literally make straight again or restore to a right state, the weakened hands and the palsied knees, in words almost reproducing the prophet. The next clause he traces to the Greek of Proverbs, quoted with some slight changes, where the verb means more probably to make even than to ponder; and he warns that the difficulty of the closing words is concealed to some extent when they are separated from the clause following, as the Authorised Version separates them, which the Greek will not allow. Robertson derives the first imperative from a compound meaning to make straight, found three times in the New Testament, and parses the two participles as perfect passives, the one of a verb meaning to let pass or relax and the other of a verb meaning to loosen at the side, to dissolve, to paralyse. The word for paths he identifies as the track of a wheel, so that the phrase asks for straight wheel-ruts; the closing clause he calls a negative final clause whose verb is an old one meaning to turn out, to twist, to put out of joint, and he judges the whole a vivid picture of concern for the lame and a graphic picture of concern for the weak.

debates: Whose hands and knees are meant: Gill takes them as the readers’ own and cites a version that reads your hands and your knees, Wesley allows either their own or their brethren’s, and Ellicott makes the whole passage a turn from personal duty to what is binding on a community.

What making the paths straight requires: Barnes and Wesley make it the removal of obstacles, for others’ feet as much as one’s own; Clarke makes it the choice of the even road rather than the clearing of it, so that an existing hurt may heal by moderate exercise; Gill makes it a rule of doctrine, the word of God alone as the rule of walking; Calvin makes it prudence, indiscreet ardour being in his judgement no less an evil than softness.

What the closing clause says of the lame: Robertson takes the verb in its physical sense of twisting or putting out of joint and reads the sentence as concern for the weak, while Wesley takes it morally, of being turned out of the way of faith and holiness, and Ellicott warns that the English conceals a difficulty by separating the clause from what precedes, which the Greek forbids.
outliers: Calvin sets a second danger against the first, holding that indiscreet ardour is no less an evil than inactivity and softness, so that the cure for discouragement must not become recklessness.
Clarke has the injured traveller healed by the road itself, a wound got in the rough way mending under moderate and equal exercise once the even path is regained.
Wesley divides the two failing members between the two figures already used in the chapter, giving the hands to the combat and the knees to the race.

14.pericope_label: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord: looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled; lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears

schools.summary: Gill enumerates the relations in which peace is to be followed — the natural and domestic, among those of the same family; the civil and political, among those of the same nation, city or society; and the spiritual, among members of the same church, or at least fellow saints though differing in some things in judgment — and extends the duty even to enemies. The next participle he explains as acting the part of bishops or overseers, as the word signifies, and asks whether the charge falls on the officers of the church, whose business it was to inspect the principles and practices of its members and see that they neither imbibed false doctrines nor lived immoral lives, or rather on the several members themselves, preferring the latter. Of the fornicator he observes that he sins against the second table of the law as well as against his own body, that the sin is opposed to the holiness just enjoined, and that such a person is not to be continued in the communion of the church. Calvin explains why the pursuit of peace needs labour: men are so born that they all seem to shun it, for all study their own interest and seek their own ways and care not to accommodate themselves to the ways of others, so that unless we strenuously labour to follow peace we shall never retain it, many things happening daily which afford occasion for discords. The participle for oversight he notes properly means overseeing, the word bishop coming from it, and he canvasses the renderings of six translators before preferring to take heed. On the two names he observes that the writer mentions a particular kind of defilement and then immediately comes to what is general by adding the profane person, that being the term strictly contrary to holiness. Of Esau he traces the sequence of mind: he at first regarded the act by which he sold his birthright as a sport, as though it were a child’s play, but at length, when too late, found what a loss he had incurred when the blessing was transferred to Jacob and refused to him — and so they who are led away by the allurements of this world alienate themselves from God and sell their own salvation.

Clarke renders the first verb as pursuing peace with the same care, attention and diligence as beasts pursue their game, following it through all places and tracing it through all winding circumstances, and having it with all men so far as one can with a safe conscience; the cultivation is to extend to Jews and Gentiles alike. The next participle he takes as looking about, over and upon, being constantly on one’s guard, and the failing as coming behind or falling off from this grace or gift of God, this state of salvation, by which he understands the gospel system or Christianity itself. He denies that Esau is charged with the first sin, since it is not intimated and the disjunctive separates the profane person from the fornicator, Esau being termed profane because he so far disregarded the spiritual advantages connected with his rights of primogeniture. The repentance he insists is not to be taken here in a theological sense as implying contrition, and he explains the rejection as Esau finding no place for a change in his father’s mind and counsel, who now perceived that it was the will of God that Jacob should be made lord of all. Wesley marks the structure of the exhortation, that this second branch concerns our neighbours and the third God, and warns that not following after all holiness is the direct way to fall into sin of every kind. The root of bitterness he specifies as envy, anger and suspicion, springing up to destroy the sweet peace, and then generalises that any corruption either in doctrine or practice is a root of bitterness and may pollute many. Esau he calls profane for so slighting the blessing which went along with the birthright, and of the repentance he says there was no room for any such as would regain what he had lost — he sought the blessing diligently and with tears, but sought too late; let us, he adds, use the present time.

Barnes takes the exhortation to peace as forbidding indulgence of the passions which lead to litigations, strifes and wars, and holds that the connection requires it to be understood mainly of persecutors, since the trials the readers were experiencing seem to have arisen chiefly from persecution. The diligent looking he says implies close attention, and there are reasons why we should take special care — the propensities of our hearts to evil, the temptations of the world, and the allurements to apostasy presented by the great adversary — while, as every man is in danger, it is his personal duty to see to it. Esau he calls a corrupt and profane man who for a trifle threw away the highest honour a son could have, and he mentions that many have regarded the first word here as referring to idolatry. Of the blessing sought afterwards he is careful: it was not that of the birthright, which Esau knew he could not regain, but that pronounced by the father on him whom he regarded as his firstborn. Ellicott renders the first clause as follow after peace, noting an allusion to the Psalm quoted also by Peter, and insists the charge is general and must not be limited to peace with fellow Christians, adding that both admonitions of this verse were admirably suited to a period of persecution. The next clause he renders whether any one be falling back from the grace of God, and observes that the defection of one member of the community brings loss and danger to the whole body; behind the root of bitterness he finds a passage of Deuteronomy plainly before the writer’s mind though not formally quoted. Of Esau he reports that Jewish tradition affirms him to have been a man of impure life but judges it not probable that he is so represented here, taking him rather as a type of the profane, who care not for divine things but only for the gains and pleasures of this world; the last verse he clarifies by placing one clause in a parenthesis, so that Esau was rejected — for he found no place of repentance — though he sought the blessing earnestly with tears. Robertson renders the first exhortation as giving peace a chase as if in a hunt, and remarks that the whole world needs this lesson, Christians included; the participle for oversight he notes occurs in the New Testament only here and in Peter and points to the noun for bishop; the failing he parses as falling short of, followed by an ablative. Profane he glosses as trodden under foot, unhallowed, and finds the idea of exchange in the phrase for one act of eating; the word for repentance he defines as a change of mind and purpose rather than sorrow, though Esau had tears afterwards, and he notes the word for the birthright occurs in the New Testament only here.

Chrysostom sets the two graces above everything else: many things are characteristic of Christianity, but more than all and better than all are love towards one another and peace, which is why Christ said he gave them his peace and made mutual love the mark by which all men should know his disciples. Cyril of Jerusalem applies the warning to a particular order, bidding the solitaries and the virgins, who maintain the angelic life in the world, be the first to give heed to the doctrine of chastity and the rest of the Church’s people follow them; a great crown, he says, is laid up, and a great dignity is not to be bartered away for a petty pleasure — as the Apostle warns, lest there be any fornicator or profane person, as Esau.

debates: How far peace with all men reaches: Barnes holds the connection requires it to be understood mainly of persecutors; Ellicott insists it is general and expressly refuses to limit it to fellow Christians; Gill enumerates every relation and extends it to enemies; Clarke adds the only qualification anyone offers, so far as one can with a safe conscience.

Whether Esau is charged with the first sin named: Clarke denies it, since the disjunctive separates the two and nothing intimates the charge; Ellicott reports that Jewish tradition does affirm Esau was of impure life but judges it improbable that he is so represented here; Barnes calls him corrupt as well as profane and notes that many have taken the first word of idolatry.

What Esau could not find: Clarke and Robertson agree the word means a change of mind and purpose rather than contrition, Clarke locating the impossibility in his father’s mind and counsel; Wesley says there was no room for a repentance that would regain what was lost; Barnes distinguishes the irrecoverable birthright from the blessing actually sought; Ellicott reaches the same sense by punctuation, making the clause a parenthesis explaining the rejection.
outliers: Clarke turns the exhortation into a hunt, pursuing peace as beasts pursue their game and tracing it through all its winding circumstances.
Calvin canvasses six translators’ renderings of a single participle before choosing his own.

Cyril of Jerusalem directs the warning first at solitaries and virgins as those who should lead the Church in chastity, and states the loss commercially — a great dignity bartered for a petty pleasure.
Robertson breaks off to say that the lesson of pursuing peace is one the whole world needs, Christians not excepted.

18.pericope_label: For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which voice they that heard intreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more: (for they could not endure that which was commanded, And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart: and so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake:)

schools.summary: Gill takes the design of the following verses to be, in general, to engage the Hebrews to adhere closely to the Gospel from the consideration of its superior excellency to the law, and in particular to enforce the earlier exhortation to cheerfulness under afflictions. Of their not enduring what was commanded he is careful to say it was not that they disliked and despised the law, as unregenerate men do, but that they could not bear it as a yoke, it being a yoke of bondage, nor as a covenant of works, since it requires perfect obedience while giving no strength to perform, and shows them their sin. The terrible sight he takes of the smoke, fire and lightnings, or of God himself who descended on the mount, citing an Arabic version which renders it that so terrible was he who vouchsafed himself to be seen. Calvin says the writer now fights with a new argument, proclaiming the greatness of the grace made known by the Gospel that we may reverently receive it, and commending to us its benign characters that he may allure us to love and desire it, adding weight to both by a comparison between the Law and the Gospel. Of the promulgation he says that when the Law was given there was nothing but terrors on every side, everything recorded in the nineteenth chapter of Exodus being of that kind and intended to show the people that God had ascended his tribunal and manifested himself as a judge.

Henry takes the apostle to be engaging the professing Hebrews to perseverance in their Christian course and conflict, and not to relapse again into Judaism, by showing how much the state of the gospel church differs from that of the Jewish church and how much it resembles the state of the church in heaven — on both accounts demanding and deserving diligence, patience and perseverance. The description of the church under the Mosaic dispensation he sums in a phrase, that it was a gross sensible state, the mountain on which that church was established being one that could be seen and handled.

Clarke insists the phrase should be translated to a palpable or material mountain, since it was not a mountain that on this occasion might be touched — the history in Exodus shows as much, and the apostle himself confirms it two verses later — so that it is called palpable as being of a material and sensible nature. Wesley reads the connective as a strong reason why they ought the more to regard the whole exhortation drawn from the priesthood of Christ, since both salvation and vengeance are now nearer at hand, and glosses the mountain as one of an earthy, material nature. The trumpet he judges was formed without doubt by the ministry of angels and was preparatory to the words, that is the Ten Commandments, uttered with a loud voice; their inability to bear he refers to the terror which seized them when they heard the words proclaimed. Of Moses he observes that even he, though admitted to so near an intercourse with God, who spake to him as a man speaketh to his friend, and though at other times acting as mediator between God and the people, stood while the ten words were pronounced as one of the hearers.

Barnes introduces the passage as a sublime comparison between the old and new dispensations, brought in to enforce the considerations already urged, its object, in accordance with the principal scope of the epistle, being to guard the readers against apostasy by showing how much more there was under the new dispensation. The trumpet sounding amid the tempest he says was fitted to increase the terror of the scene, and it is easy to conceive what awe must have been produced by a voice uttered from the midst of the tempest yet so distinct as to be heard by the hundreds of thousands present. Of their not enduring he explains that the meaning is not that the commands themselves were intolerable, but that the manner in which they were communicated inspired a terror they could not bear, so that they feared they should die. On the words attributed to Moses he raises the difficulty plainly: this is not recorded in the account of the giving of the law in Exodus, and it has been made a question on what authority the apostle made the declaration, though Moses does say something of the kind in Deuteronomy, after he had come down from the mountain and broken the two tables. Ellicott supplies the source of each phrase — the voice of the trumpet, the voice of the words — and the terms of the entreaty, that if they heard the voice of the Lord their God any more they should die; though God drew near to Israel to reveal himself, so terrible was his voice to them and so awful the penalties which fenced the mountain round. He judges there is no sufficient reason for enclosing these two verses in a parenthesis, prefers to render the next clause if even a beast touch the mountain it shall be stoned, and notes that the following words about being thrust through with a dart are absent from our best authorities and have accidentally found their way into the text from Exodus. On the saying of Moses he observes that the Greek of Deuteronomy contains these words in part, but that there they belong to a later time, when Moses was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure of the Lord. Robertson notes there is no word here in the Greek for a mount, as there is in the following verses and in the Old Testament passages, though one is clearly understood since the datives agree with it, unless the participles are taken as descriptive of the fire. The word for blackness he calls a late form akin to the word for cloud, occurring only here in the New Testament and quoted from Exodus, and the word for darkness an old one used by Homer for the gloom of the world below; the verb for their not enduring he parses as an imperfect, they were not enduring, and the participle from an old verb meaning to distinguish, to dispose, to order. The adjective for fearful he notes occurs in the New Testament only in this epistle, and the participle for the appearance only here, rendering it the manifestation.

Chrysostom grants the awe on both sides before marking the difference: wonderful indeed were the things in the Temple, the Holy of Holies, and awful too were the things done at Mount Sinai — the fire, the darkness, the blackness, the tempest — for it is said that God appeared in Sinai, and long ago were these things celebrated; the New Covenant, however, was not given with such accompaniments. Cyril of Jerusalem turns from the mountain to the incarnation: these things the Jews read but do not hear, for they have stopped the ears of their heart that they may not hear; but let us believe in Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh and been made man, because we could not receive him otherwise — since we could not look upon or enjoy him as he was, he became what we are, that we might so receive him.

debates: Whether the mountain could be touched: Clarke insists the rendering must be a palpable or material mountain precisely because it was not one that might then be touched, the history and the apostle both forbidding it, while Robertson observes that the Greek supplies no noun for a mount at all and the word must be understood from the agreement of the datives.

What it was that they could not endure: Barnes says the commands themselves were not intolerable and locates the terror in the manner of their communication, whereas Gill locates it in the law itself, as a yoke of bondage and a covenant of works requiring perfect obedience while giving no strength to perform.

Where the words attributed to Moses come from: Barnes states plainly that they are not in the Exodus narrative and that the apostle’s authority for them has been questioned; Ellicott finds part of them in the Greek of Deuteronomy but belonging to a later occasion, when Moses feared the anger of the Lord; Gill and Wesley take the terror as Sinai’s without raising the difficulty.
outliers: Ellicott makes two editorial judgements in one verse, denying that the passage needs a parenthesis and holding that a clause of the received text entered it accidentally from Exodus and is absent from the best authorities.
Robertson identifies the word for darkness as the one Homer uses for the gloom of the world below.
Wesley notes that during the giving of the ten words Moses stood not as mediator but as one of the hearers, though at other times he was mediator between God and the people.
Cyril of Jerusalem leaves the mountain for the incarnation, arguing that Christ became what we are because we could not look upon him as he was.

22.pericope_label: But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel

schools.summary: Gill takes Mount Sion and the other names given here to mean the church of God under the Gospel dispensation, to which the believing Hebrews were already come, and reports the reading of the Alexandrian copy which may seem to favour the interpretation referring the passage to the heavenly state, to which saints in this present life are not yet come. The general assembly he explains from Greek usage as a public and solemn convention held at games, feasts, fairs or on religious accounts, signifying a large collection and convention of men and sometimes the place where they met, and applies it to the church of God consisting of all his elect, both Jews and Gentiles. Of the last clause he says that coming to Christ is by faith, and is different both from a corporeal coming to him in the days of his flesh and from an outward attendance on ordinances, being a coming under a sense of want and upon a sight of fulness, and the produce of God’s efficacious grace. Calvin hears in the name an allusion to the prophecies in which God had promised that his Gospel should go forth from Zion, and observes that the writer contrasts that mountain with Sinai and expressly calls it heavenly, so that the Jews might not cleave to what was earthly and had flourished under the Law. Of the firstborn he says the term is not given to the children of God indiscriminately, since Scripture calls many his children who are not of that number, but is used for the sake of honour to adorn the patriarchs and other renowned saints of the ancient Church; the enrolment in heaven he refers to God’s having all the elect written in his book or secret catalogue. The final clause he explains as placed last because it is through Christ alone that the Father is reconciled to us and renders his face serene and lovely to us, so that we may come to him without fear; and the phrase about sprinkling he takes, after the Hebrew mode of speaking, to mean sprinkled blood.

Clarke sets out the imagery, that the Church, here called the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem and Mount Sion, is represented under the notion of a city, and that the great assembly of believers in Christ is opposed to the congregation of the Israelites assembled at Mount Sinai. Of the general assembly he reports that the word is joined to the preceding clause by some of the best manuscripts and quoted in that connection by several of the fathers, so that the sense is that they are come to the general assembly of innumerable angels, which he judges probably the true connection; the word itself he derives from those for all and for an assembly and takes of a gathering collected on festive occasions. Of the last verses he says the old covenant and its mediator Moses are passed away, while the new covenant, that is the Gospel, is now in force and will be to the end of the world, its mediator being the Son of God, the Maker and Preserver of all things and the Saviour and Judge of all men. Wesley denies that the apostle here speaks of their coming to the church militant, taking it instead of the glorious privilege of New Testament believers, their communion with the church triumphant, which is far more apparent to the eyes of celestial spirits than to ours, which are yet veiled. The general assembly he calls properly a stated convention on some festival occasion, and the church the whole body of true believers whether on earth or in paradise; the firstborn of Israel were enrolled by Moses, but these are enrolled in heaven as citizens there, and he observes that in this beautiful gradation the firstborn are placed nearer to God than the angels named before them. The blood of sprinkling he takes as all the virtue of the precious blood shed for them, whereby they are sprinkled from an evil conscience, and calls it the foundation of our Lord’s mediatorial office, the gradation being here at its highest point; the better things it speaks he sets against the blood of Abel, which cried for vengeance.

Barnes takes the design to be a contrast of the Christian dispensation with the Jewish, showing that its excellences and advantages were far superior to the religion of their fathers, having more to win the affections and to elevate and inspire with hope, and less that was terrific and alarming. The firstborn he explains from Hebrew custom, since those who were firstborn enjoyed peculiar privileges and especially pre-eminence of rank, and refers the phrase evidently to those saints who had been distinguished for their piety and may be supposed exalted to peculiar honours. The Mediator he calls the crowning excellence of the new dispensation in contradistinction from the old, since the readers had been made acquainted with the true Messiah, were united to him by faith and had been sprinkled with his blood. Ellicott insists that in these difficult verses it is unusually important to follow the literal rendering of the Greek, and gives it as Zion the mountain and city of a Living God, a heavenly Jerusalem, noting that the thought of a celestial city which should be the exact counterpart of the earthly Jerusalem is often dwelt upon in Jewish writings, so that the writer is using familiar words. The next phrase he renders according to what the order of the Greek seems to require, a Judge who is God of all, and marks the turn of thought: to this point it has rested on the heavenly world and those who from the time of their creation have been its inhabitants, whereas men who have passed through this earthly life have no essential right to citizenship in the heavenly Jerusalem and come first before a Judge. On the covenant he notes another change in the Greek which is not easy to express, since in all other places where the New Covenant is spoken of a word is used implying newness of kind and quality, while here it is a covenant which is newly made. Robertson marks the sharp contrast with the earlier verse, the same verb form standing in both, and observes that heaven is here termed a spiritual mountain and city, as Paul contrasts the present Jerusalem with the Jerusalem above in Galatians. The word for general assembly he calls an old one found only here in the New Testament, notes that the related verb is used in Isaiah of keeping a festal holiday, and allows that it may possibly be connected with the angels, though this is not certain; the church of the firstborn he takes as probably an additional item beside the angelic host, the people of Israel being themselves called firstborn. Of the last clauses he says the great fact of coming to Jesus is not to be overlooked, since he is there as Lord and Saviour and still Jesus, and that the mediation of a new covenant, already shown in the epistle, is now gloriously consummated.

Cyril of Jerusalem recalls that of old the Psalmist sang that God should be blessed in the congregations, but that after the Jews were cast away from grace for the plots they made against the Saviour, he built out of the Gentiles a second holy Church, the Church of us Christians, concerning which he said to Peter that upon this rock he would build his Church.

debates: Whether the coming is present or future: Gill takes it of the gospel church under the present dispensation and reports the manuscript reading that would favour the other view, while Wesley expressly denies that the church militant is meant and makes it the believer’s communion with the church triumphant, a thing more apparent to celestial spirits than to us.

Where the general assembly belongs: Clarke joins it to the preceding clause on the authority of the best manuscripts and several of the fathers, so that it is the angels who form the festal gathering, and calls this probably the true connection; Robertson allows the connection as possible but not certain and treats the church of the firstborn as an additional item.

Who the firstborn are: Calvin denies the title to God’s children indiscriminately and reserves it as an honour for the patriarchs and renowned saints of the ancient Church; Wesley extends it to the whole body of true believers on earth or in paradise; Barnes takes them as saints distinguished for piety and exalted to peculiar honours.
outliers: Ellicott warns that in these verses it is unusually important to follow the literal Greek, and finds that the word for new here means newly made rather than new in kind and quality, as it does everywhere else the New Covenant is named.
Wesley reads the order of the list as a gradation and observes that the firstborn are placed nearer to God than the innumerable angels named before them.
Robertson refuses to let the name pass unremarked in the middle of the catalogue, noting that he stands there as Lord and Saviour and still as Jesus.

25.pericope_label: See that ye refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven: whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven … Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear: for our God is a consuming fire

schools.summary: Gill takes the speaker to be Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant, whose blood speaks better things than Abel’s, and traces his speaking through the council and covenant of grace, where he spoke for the elect, and through the creation of all things out of nothing. He holds that Christ was present at the giving of the law and that his voice was then heard, whether the voice of thunder or of the trumpet or rather the voice of words, which shook Sinai and the land about it and the people on it. On the closing sentence he keeps the two aspects together in one person: Christ is truly God, and he is our God and Lord, and though he is full of grace and mercy he will appear in great wrath to his enemies who will not have him to reign over them. Calvin observes that the writer uses the same verb as before, when the people entreated that God should not speak to them, but means another thing by it, that we ought not to reject the word destined for us, and shows what he had in view in the last comparison, that the severest punishment awaits the despisers of the Gospel. Though God shook the earth when he published his Law, he says, he now speaks more gloriously, since he shakes both earth and heaven; the prophet is quoted on the subject though not in his own words. He is careful about the quotation: the prophet’s words are yet a little while, and he meant that the calamity of the people would not be perpetual but that the Lord would succour them, whereas the Apostle lays no stress on that expression and infers only from the shaking of heaven and earth that the state of the world was to be changed at the coming of Christ. On the last verse he marks the method: as the writer had before kindly set before us the grace of God, so he now makes known his severity, borrowing the sentence from Deuteronomy — God omitting nothing by which he may draw us to himself, and beginning with love and kindness so that we may follow him the more willingly.

Clarke identifies the speaker as the Lord Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, who now speaks from heaven by his Gospel to Jews and Gentiles alike, having in his incarnation come down from God, and the one who spoke on earth as Moses, who spoke on God’s part to the Hebrews. From this he infers that it seems to have been the voice of Jesus which then shook the earth and that it was he who came down on the mount, though he records that others refer the words simply to God the Father giving the law. The removal he reads historically, of the whole Jewish polity, which had been in a shaken state from the time that Judea fell under the power of the Romans, and he takes the things that are made as subjects intended to last only for a time, God never having designed that the Jewish religion should become general. The kingdom he identifies with the Gospel dispensation, frequently termed the kingdom of God and of heaven because in it God reigns among men and in the hearts of them that believe, its character being righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Ghost, and which cannot be moved because it can never fail. From the closing quotation he teaches the great truth that sin under the Gospel is as abominable in God’s sight as it was under the law, and that the man who does not labour to serve God in the way prescribed will find that fire to consume him. Wesley takes the refusing to be by unbelief and observes that the present speaking is a prelude to the final scene, since the same voice which spoke both by the law and in the gospel, when heard from heaven, will shake heaven and earth. The promise he calls joyful to the saints though dreadful to the wicked; the things shaken he identifies as heaven and earth, which being made are consequently liable to change, so that what remains is the new heaven and the new earth. The receiving he makes an act of willing and joyful faith and the kingdom more glorious than the present heaven and earth; the holding fast of grace he takes as a serving of God in every thought, word and work, and the reverence asked for he renders literally as shame, arising from a deep consciousness of our own unworthiness, with a tender and jealous fear beside it. The consuming fire he refers to the strictness of God’s justice and the purity of his holiness.

Barnes takes the speaker to be God addressing them in the gospel, holding that he has spoken to them there as really as he had spoken to the Hebrews at Mount Sinai, and warns against turning away from one who has called them to obey and serve him. The shaking he refers to the quaking of the mountain and the region around it, and identifies the words that follow as taken from Haggai. The explanation of the prophecy he states as a general rule: there would be such agitations that everything not fixed on a permanent and immovable basis would be thrown down as in an earthquake. The kingdom he calls permanent and unchanging, not, like the Jewish dispensation, to give place to another, nor destructible by any power; and the closing quotation from Deuteronomy he takes as a further reason why God should be served with profound reverence and unwavering fidelity, the object being to show that there was the same reason for fearing him now as then. Ellicott notes that the word for refusing occurs twice in this verse in the sense of declining to listen, with clear reference to the earlier verse in which the Israelites deprecated the speaking of more words, and takes the speaker to be God speaking to us. The terrors of Sinai he makes a type of a more terrible revelation of judgment, when not only shall the earth tremble but the earth and the heaven shall be moved and all that is transitory and mutable shall pass away, the words of Haggai being taken as a prophecy of this. The phrase yet once more he holds equivalent to once more only, so that the words must of necessity point to the final change which issues in the removal of all that can pass away, and he renders the following clause literally as which are not shaken. The kingdom he refers clearly to the promise in Daniel that the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, with the closing verses of the same chapter of Haggai also before the writer’s mind; and of the last sentence he notes that in Deuteronomy these words follow a solemn warning against idolatry. Robertson calls the opening imperative an earnest word which drives home the whole argument of the epistle by the powerful contrast between the two mountains, and states the consequence: the consequences are dreadful to apostates now, for Zion has greater terrors than Sinai, great as those were. The perfect tense of the promise he notes still holds, and the article before the quoted phrase is used to point it out before it is explained; he quotes the judgement that there is a divine purpose in the cosmic catastrophe. The last exhortation he calls the ground of loyalty to Christ and of calm trust in God, and renders it as a continuing action, let us keep on having grace; the closing participle he notes occurs only here in the New Testament, and couples the verse with an earlier one of the same epistle.

Chrysostom sets the exhortation beside another of the same kind, that the things which are seen are temporal while the things which are not seen are eternal, from which the same writer elsewhere draws an exhortation about the evils we endure in this present life; here, he says, the writer does the same, bidding us continue steadfast and have thankfulness.

debates: Who it is that speaks: Gill and Clarke both take it of Christ, Clarke completing the contrast by identifying the earthly speaker as Moses, while Barnes and Ellicott make the speaker God addressing us in the gospel.
Whose voice shook the earth at Sinai: Gill holds that Christ was present and his voice then heard, and Clarke infers the same while recording that others refer the words simply to God the Father.

What the removal amounts to: Clarke reads it historically of the Jewish polity, already shaking under Roman power, and denies that God ever designed that religion to become general; Ellicott insists the words must of necessity point to the final change and the removal of everything that can pass away; Wesley makes the things shaken heaven and earth, replaced by the new; Barnes states it as a rule, that whatever is not on a permanent basis is thrown down.
outliers: Robertson turns the chapter’s comparison round at the end, holding that the consequences are now worse rather than milder, since Zion has greater terrors than Sinai, great as those were.

Calvin points out that the prophet’s own words are yet a little while and that they were spoken as comfort about a passing calamity, and observes that the Apostle lays no stress on the expression at all, resting his inference solely on the shaking.
Wesley renders the reverence required as literally shame, arising from a deep consciousness of our own unworthiness.
Calvin describes the writer’s method rather than his doctrine, that God begins with love and kindness so that we may follow him the more willingly and produces his severity only afterwards.
